observations: A rounded head shape occupies the right half, rendered in olive and amber wash, with a tight white spiral marking one eye socket and a row of pale rectangular forms along the lower jaw edge.
The left side divides between a black field carrying white dripped and angular marks and a dense tangle of red, orange, green and black lines filling the upper dome of the head.
Along the bottom, thick yellow vertical bars with dripping ends sit against a dark olive ground, forming a distinct horizontal band separate from the figure above.
reading: The head sits in three-quarter view, its left side dissolving into layered scribble while the right eye socket holds a coiled white spiral that draws the eye inward. The black zone beside it reads as an abrupt cutaway, and the dripping yellow bars below carry a different quality — flat, repeated, unhurried. The image holds tension between the dense interior marks and those spare bottom forms.
contextAngle: Within the owned nnotb subset, this work sits between nnotb #69 and nnotb #71 in both title and recorded creation order. Where #69 spreads a skull form across a warm busy field with red X marks, #70 compresses the figure and introduces an isolated yellow bar row absent in either neighbor.

connections.reason: Both center a rounded skull-like head in amber and olive with dense overlaid lines, but #69 scatters marks across the full field while #70 concentrates them inside the dome and isolates the lower bar band.

nifty faces #128 shares a large single eye rendered as a pale oval against a dark surround and exposed tooth-like forms low in the composition, though it places them on a flat pink ground rather than within layered marks.

lookingQuestion: What does the relationship between the tight spiral in the eye socket and the evenly spaced yellow bars at the bottom do to how you move through the image?
ambiguities: The pale rectangular forms along the lower jaw edge read as teeth but could be abstract marks; no external confirmation available.
The nifty faces #128 comparison is cross-collection and rests on visible formal overlap only; no evidence links the two works beyond what is seen in the images.
